title: Childhood Adversity Dimensions and Brain Signatures During Reward Processing in Adolescents: A Systematic Review of Task-Based fMRI Studies
abstract: Accumulating evidence suggests that childhood adversity disrupts reward-related brain function and may contribute to increased risk for psychopathology in adolescence. This systematic review aimed to synthesize neuroimaging evidence on how childhood adversity affects reward processing across adolescence (10–24 years). We conducted a comprehensive search of task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging studies published before July 2025 in databases including PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycINFO. A total of 11 eligible studies were included, all examining trauma-exposed adolescents’ neural responses to reward. Findings revealed consistent functional changes in key regions of the reward circuitry, including ventral striatum (VS), prefrontal cortex (PFC), and amygdala. These alterations varied across trauma subtype and reward phase. Abuse was commonly associated with increased activation in emotion-related regions such as the amygdala and ventrolateral PFC, whereas neglect was linked to reduced responsivity in reward circuits including VS and caudate nucleus. Additionally, during the reward anticipation phase, trauma-exposed youth showed diminished activity in the VS, caudate, and posterior cingulate cortex, while reward feedback was associated with increased activation in social-cognitive regions such as the ventromedial PFC and temporoparietal junction. A subset of studies identified the reward system as a potential mediator or moderator between trauma and later psychological outcomes. These findings provide preliminary support for incorporating specific trauma assessment approaches (e.g., differentiating distinct subtypes and evaluating cumulative severity) and reward-phase-specific neural markers into risk identification and intervention strategies for youth across the adolescent developmental span.
